summary_html: A **parent/guardian/child requests help** without a substantiated allegation. FFPSA created a federal pathway for **prevention services** to avert removal and stabilize families before a case escalates.
authority_html: - **Family First Prevention Services Act (2018)** — prevention services, kinship support; shifts upstream from removal to support

primary_citations.citation_text: Hawaii — HRS Chapter 587A, Child Protective Act
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 350-1.1, Reports (persons required to report child abuse or neglect)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E.
key_cases.holding: The court held that the presumption that a fit parent acts in the child's best interest survives the parent's consent to a guardianship, and that article I, sections 5 and 6 of the Hawai'i Constitution require clear and convincing evidence of unfitness before that presumption may be set aside.
key_cases.relevance: A parent who voluntarily asks for help by consenting to a guardianship does not thereby waive the constitutional presumption in their favor.
key_cases.quote: the rebuttable presumption that a fit parent acts in the best interest of their child extends to guardianship proceedings

key_cases.holding: The court held that the family court lacked jurisdiction to order the Department of Health to fund services where IDEA remedies were unexhausted, but that the child's status as a ward of the State created an independent state-law basis obligating the State, with DHS ultimately accountable, to pay for his mental health services.
key_cases.relevance: Foster families who seek help for a child in their care have a state-law route to funded services independent of federal education law.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the family court correctly concluded that an independent state basis exists under which John is entitled to receive payment for the mental health services

key_cases.case_name: In re the Guardianship of Doe
key_cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
key_cases.holding: The ICA held that in deciding whether to terminate or continue a non-parent's guardianship of a minor the family court must consider the parental preference of HRS § 571-46(1) within the best-interests inquiry, adopting for Hawai'i a rebuttable custody presumption in favor of parents, but affirmed continuation of the grandparents' guardianship because the family court implicitly considered that preference and the evidence supported its order.
key_cases.relevance: This is the origin of the rebuttable parental presumption in Hawai'i guardianship practice that In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E. later grounded in article I, sections 5 and 6, so a parent who seeks or consents to a guardianship starts from that presumption.
key_cases.quote: we believe our jurisdiction is similar to the majority of jurisdictions which adopt a custody presumption in favor of parents subject to rebuttal

key_cases.case_name: In re the Guardianship of Doe
key_cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
key_cases.holding: The ICA held that the heightened clear and convincing standard of proof required to terminate parental rights does not apply to the parental-fitness question in a minor guardianship proceeding, because a guardianship of the person of a minor is neither absolute nor irrevocable, and it vacated the denial of the grandparents' co-guardianship petition and remanded for reconsideration.
key_cases.relevance: It held that parental fitness in a guardianship need not be proved by clear and convincing evidence — precisely the rule In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E. displaced on state constitutional grounds in 2026 — so anyone relying on pre-2026 guardianship authority must check this holding first.
key_cases.quote: We conclude the family court erred in applying a heightened standard of proof to the question of the fitness of the natural father.

state_agency.name: Hawaii Department of Human Services, Child Welfare Services
state_agency.hotline: 808-832-5300 (Oahu) or toll-free 1-888-380-3088 (Hawaii Island, Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kauai), 24 hours a day, 7 days a week

mandatory_reporters: Licensed or registered professionals of the healing arts or any health-related occupation who examine, attend, treat, or provide other professional or specialized services, including but not limited to physicians (including physicians in training), psychologists, dentists, nurses, osteopathic physicians and surgeons, optometrists, chiropractors, podiatrists, pharmacists, and other health-related professionals
Employees or officers of any public or private school
Employees or officers of any public or private agency or institution, or other individuals, providing social, medical, hospital, or mental health services, including financial assistance

Employees or officers of any law enforcement agency, including but not limited to the courts, police departments, department of law enforcement, correctional institutions, and parole or probation offices
Individual providers of child care, or employees or officers of any licensed or registered child care facility, foster home, or similar institution
Employees of any public or private agency providing recreational or sports activities
Commercial film and photographic print or image processors

Members of the clergy or custodians of records therefor; a member of the clergy is not required to report information gained solely during a penitential communication, except when the clergy member believes that there exists a substantial risk that child abuse or neglect that is especially heinous, atrocious, or cruel, manifesting exceptional depravity, may occur in the reasonably foreseeable future, and a clergy member who receives reportable information from any source other than a penitential communication must report it regardless of whether the same information was also received during a penitential communication
reporting_details: Hawaii is not a universal-reporting state: only the ten categories of persons listed in Haw. Rev. Stat. § 350-1.1(a) must report, and they must report the matter immediately and orally to the Department of Human Services or the police, with a written report to follow (§ 350-1.1(c)); anyone else may report voluntarily under § 350-1.3.
